content: 1. If a pesticide product is associated with multiple GHS health hazards, specific rules govern the precedence of symbols and signal words on the label. For example, if the skull-and-crossbones symbol is used for one hazard, the exclamation mark for another hazard should not appear. Similarly, if the corrosive symbol is used, the exclamation mark should not be displayed for skin or eye irritation. If the health hazard symbol is used for respiratory sensitization, the exclamation mark should not be used for skin sensitization or skin/eye irritation. 2. All assigned hazard statements must be included on the label, except in cases where H314 (causes severe skin burns and eye damage) is assigned, in which case H318 (causes serious eye damage) may be omitted. 3. If hazard color bands are displayed on the label and the pesticide product poses more than one GHS health hazard, only the most hazardous color band should be shown. 4. Pesticides that exhibit germ cell mutagenicity, carcinogenicity, reproductive toxicity, or specific target organ systemic toxicity after repeated exposure are generally not authorized for use in most countries. However, if they are authorized, appropriate hazard labeling must be implemented. 5. Aspiration hazards are recognized under GHS classification and should be labeled accordingly. It is not recommended to mix GHS classification with WHO classification for pesticide labeling to avoid conflicts and user confusion. A single classification system (either GHS or WHO) should be applied consistently within a country. 6. Human health risk assessments for pesticide use may necessitate the inclusion of specific precautionary statements and pictograms on the label, addressing both GHS-covered hazards and broader risks such as effects on wildlife, pollinators, and soil organisms. 7. The WHO classification system differs from GHS in its criteria and classes. While WHO classification is still used in many countries, the transition to GHS is recommended for harmonized classification and labeling of pesticides. Countries transitioning from WHO to GHS should do so at a fixed date for all pesticide labels, providing sufficient advance notice to manufacturers and distributors. 8. During the transition, authorities should inform users about changes in hazard symbols, signal words, and hazard statements. Mixing WHO and GHS classifications is not advisable, as it may lead to inconsistencies between labels and Safety Data Sheets (SDS). 9. Environmental hazards under GHS currently include only aquatic toxicity and ozone layer hazards. For labeling purposes, the pesticide formulation or end-user product should be classified, not just the active ingredient. If multiple GHS environmental hazards are present, precedence rules apply to hazard statements on the label. 10. Pesticide labels alone are often insufficient to ensure proper use, safety precautions, or emergency responses. Risk communication strategies, such as posters, media campaigns, and training programs, should complement labeling efforts, especially in populations with limited literacy or education. 11. Governments and the pesticide industry should establish systems to regularly inform and train users on proper pesticide use, label comprehension, and risk management. Introducing pesticide label education into school curricula could provide a more sustained approach. 12. Authorities should ensure compliance with national labeling regulations through inspections and enforcement. Inspectors should report issues with labels and comprehension to improve their effectiveness.
